name: Serbian folk dance

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A member of a local Cultural Artistic Society.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Wheel of Serbia: Understanding the Kolo
This is Serbian folk dance. 19th century to present.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Title card: Serbian folk dance · Serbia · 19th century to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Kolo dances originated in different parts of Serbia, shaped by local traditions, historical influences, and migration patterns.
The tradition is a collective practice that has been documented since at least the 19th century, with specific dances like Moravac and Kukunjest recorded in Central Serbia during that era.
on_screen: Map: Serbia · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Kolo is a social dance used to celebrate community events.
It is a collective expression of unity, and in the case of the Šetnja, it was historically used to gather people into a growing chain during festivities.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Serbian Folk Dance (Balkan Folk Fest 2018) [WWW.ETOILE.APP] (https://archive.org/details/serbian-folk-dance-balkan-folk-fest-2018-www.-etoile.-app)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Kolo is danced in a closed or open circle with dancers holding hands in a V or W formation.
The kolovodja leads the group.
Steps are often laterally symmetrical, involving triple steps, cross steps, and hops.
Watch for Triple step, Hop.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Closed or open circle, moving laterally.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is typically characterized by lively melodies in major scales.
Common time signatures include 2/4, 3/4, 7/8, and 7/16.
Listen for the accordion.
Lively major-scale melodies often played on the accordion, characterized by rhythmic consistency that aligns with the 8-measure dance structure.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers often wear full traditional costumes when performing on stage.
The dance occurs at weddings, festivals, and social gatherings in both urban and rural settings.
on_screen: Image gallery: 6 licensed images with attribution
Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Milija Spasojević, an accordionist who composed the melody for Užičko kolo in 1962.
Saša Mutic, who composed the Robot Kolo in 1984.
Variants include the Šumadija-based Kolo in three steps, the northern Banat Malo Kolo, the eastern Serbian Rumenka Kolo, and the southeastern Čačak Kolo.
The tradition is part of the broader Slavic folk dance family, with influences from regional interactions and historical legacies.

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
